newsitem.title: INDIA: India's striking truck owners stand firm.
newsitem.headline: India's striking truck owners stand firm.

text.p: Striking Indian truck owners stood firm on Friday after the government asked the army to help to move goods stranded on the fourth day of a nationwide protest that has pushed up prices, transport officials said.
The strike has kept more than two million trucks off the roads and crippled the delivery of goods on roads and through ports and air cargo terminals.
Shortages have begun to emerge, pushing up prices of essential and perishable commodities, and business leaders said the strike could harm the entire economy.
But strike leaders said they would not back down from their demand that the government scrap a proposed service tax and sharp rise in insurance premiums.
"We have no choice but to continue with the strike," S.P. Singh, a spokesman for the All India Motor Transport Congress (AIMTC), told Reuters.
"The strike will continue till our demands are met."
The AIMTC represents owners of about two million heavy trucks, one million light and medium-weight trucks and 60,000 booking and delivery companies. Truckers move almost two thirds of India's goods.

The government on Thursday sought the army's help and asked states to invoke the Essential Services Act, which empowers authorities to declare the movement of goods an essential service and take punitive action against those blocking it.
The truck owners scoffed at the government's move.

"The government is trying to turn it into a law-and-order situation. We have asked our people to stay calm," said Singh. "The ball was in the government's court. The government has to come back to us with their proposals."
The transport industry is losing four billion rupees ($112 million) a day from the strike, Singh said.
Industry and trade officials have urged the truck owners to call off the strike as the prices of essential goods are rising.
"In case the strike continues for a few more days, the prices would scale up further," said Krishan Kumar Bansal, the president of Foodgrain Dealers Association.
Small producers, who typically have low inventories, and exporters have been hard hit and fear substantial losses if the strike drags on.
"Manufacturing is being affected, raw materials are not reaching the factories," a spokesman for the Punjab, Haryana, Delhi Chambers of Commerce and Industry (PHDCCI) said.
"Many factories are closing. Exports have stopped as goods movement has come to a grinding halt," the spokesman said.
India's major ports, particularly Bombay, have been severely affected and there is no movement of goods at the docks, government officials said.
The petroleum industry will be also affected if the strike continues for a few more days, said an official of the state-run Indian Oil Corporation (IOC).
"The consumer is not affected right now. But the situation is problematic in south India and the northeast," the IOC official said.
